newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Little celebration in Nigeria's inflation victory.
newsitem.headline: Little celebration in Nigeria's inflation victory.

text.p: News that Nigeria's year-on-year inflation has slipped below double digits for the first time in more than six years is cause for only muted celebration, business operators said on Thursday.

The latest victory of the Nigerian military rulers in their declared war on infaltion, the perceived scourge of black Africa's largest economy, has been won at the price of prolonging recession, they said.

"The one good sign in this is that perhaps they may relax their policy a little now that they appear to be on target and we might see some reflationary spending," said one banker in the commercial capital Lagos.
Figures from the Federal Office of Statistics on Wednesday showed that inflation dropped to 9.9 percent year-on-year in May from 14.2 percent a month earlier and 31.0 percent the year before.

The average of the 12 months, used by the finance ministry to set its economic targets, stood at 19.3 percent, down from 21.0 percent the previous month. The ministry has targeted an average figure of 15 percent for the year.
Analysts say they expect a blip in the June figure, due to fuel shortages during the month which pushed up the price of transport and the cost of bringing food from farms in the interior.
Even so, tight fiscal policies of General Sani Abacha and finance minister Anthony Ani appear on target, they say.
"Yes, but at what price?" asked food importer Koffor Osomo. "If nobody has money to spend what is the point of shouting about figures?"

Suckled by exports of more than two million barrels per day of crude oil, Africa's most populous nation of 104 million people soon feels the pinch when government decides to tighten the purse strings.

So far it has not yet approved a capital expenditure budget for 1997, let alone released the money. Foreign oil companies in joint venture partnerships complain their budgets have been cut and production and exploration will suffer.

The Petroleum Trust Fund, set up to cushion the blow of fuel price rises through infrastructure and social projects, has not been spending since a flurry last year which fuelled inflation and put pressure on the now stable naira currency.

"The pursuit of further reduction in the inflation rate...is excellent, but the side effects of these measures on the economic well-being of the citizenry should also be taken into consideration," Bassey Ndiokho, the managing director of conglomerate UAC said recently.
Decades of addiction to crude oil have left Nigeria's economy unable to turn quickly to former alternative exports such as cocoa, oilseeds and rubber.

The ruling generals have so far shunned privatisation of the oil industry and inefficient state-run enterprises, which both local business and international lenders have recommended to encourage growth.

The reluctance to show more commitment to reforms like privatisation and ending dual exchange rates has become another sticking point in relations with Western countries, whih are already unhappy about alleged human rights abuses and unsure about a planned handover to civilian rule in 1998.
Abacha took over in the turmoil after the annulment of the last presidential elections by the military in 1993, vowing to restore both political and economic stability to the often chaotic nation.
